DIY Termite Control: What Works & What Doesn't (2024)

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

DIY Termite Control: What Actually Works and What Doesn't

If you're searching for termite control DIY solutions, you're probably hoping to save money and handle a termite problem yourself. That's understandable—professional treatment isn't cheap. But here's the honest truth from someone who's been treating termites in Kansas since 1987: most DIY termite products sold at hardware stores won't eliminate an active infestation, especially the subterranean termites common in Wichita and surrounding areas. Some DIY approaches work as preventive measures, but active colonies require a different level of intervention. At Shaw's Pest Control, we hold three state certifications and a Master Tech Certification, and we've seen countless homeowners waste time and money on products that can't reach the root of the problem. This guide will show you what works, what doesn't, and when it's time to call in professionals.

What Makes DIY Termite Control So Challenging

Termite control differs fundamentally from other pest problems because you're not just dealing with the insects you see—you're fighting an entire colony that may contain hundreds of thousands of termites hidden in the ground or behind walls. Subterranean termites, the species that cause 95% of termite damage in Kansas, build their colonies underground and travel through mud tubes to reach wood in your home. When you spot termite damage or see winged termites (swarmers), you're only seeing a tiny fraction of the problem.

Most DIY termite products fall into two categories: spot treatments and barrier treatments. Spot treatments include foams, sprays, and termiticide concentrates you apply directly to visible termite activity. Barrier treatments involve applying liquid termiticide around your home's foundation to create a chemical barrier. The problem? Spot treatments rarely reach the queen and the main colony, so the infestation continues. Barrier treatments require precise application rates, extensive trenching, and hundreds of gallons of properly mixed termiticide—something nearly impossible to achieve correctly without professional equipment. Missing even a small section of the barrier gives termites a highway right back into your home.

The One DIY Approach That Actually Works: Borate Wood Treatment

If you're looking for a legitimate DIY termite control method, borate-based wood treatments are your best option—but with significant limitations. Borates (like disodium octaborate tetrahydrate) are minerals that penetrate wood and become toxic to termites when they consume it. Products like Bora-Care, Tim-bor, and similar borate solutions can be brushed or sprayed onto bare wood surfaces to create long-lasting protection.

Here's what makes borates effective: they're not repellent like many other termiticides, so termites don't avoid treated wood—they consume it and die. Borates also remain in the wood for years, providing ongoing protection. The catch? Borates only work on exposed, untreated wood, and they won't eliminate an existing colony. You can only apply them to bare wood, so they're most useful in crawl spaces, unfinished basements, or during new construction or renovation projects. Once wood is painted, finished, or covered, borate treatment becomes impractical.

Borate treatments work well for prevention but won't solve an active infestation. They don't spread through a colony like modern termiticide transfer agents, and they can't reach the queen or the main nest underground. If you have existing termite damage or active swarmers, borate treatments might protect untreated wood but won't stop the colony attacking your home. For comprehensive termite control in Wichita, you'll need a treatment that targets the entire colony system.

Why Most Store-Bought Termite Products Fall Short

Walk into any hardware store and you'll find shelves of termite control products: sprays, baits, foams, and granules. Most homeowners buy these hoping for an easy solution, but the reality is disappointing. Termite foam and spray products typically contain low concentrations of active ingredients (often pyrethroids like bifenthrin or cypermethrin) that kill termites on contact but don't transfer through the colony. You might kill a few dozen or even a few hundred termites, but the colony of several hundred thousand continues thriving underground.

Liquid termiticide concentrates sold at hardware stores face different problems. Professional-grade termiticides are regulated and often unavailable to homeowners, so retail products contain lower concentrations or different active ingredients. More importantly, proper application requires specialized equipment: tank sprayers capable of delivering dozens of gallons, trenching tools, and knowledge of exactly where and how to apply the product. Most DIY applications create incomplete barriers with gaps that termites easily circumvent.

Termite bait stations represent another popular DIY option, but they come with challenges. While professional bait systems like those used in comprehensive termite treatment programs can effectively eliminate colonies, store-bought versions often contain less palatable baits or lower concentrations of active ingredients. More critically, effective baiting requires proper station placement, regular monitoring, and patience—it can take months for a colony to consume enough bait to die off. Most homeowners install bait stations incorrectly, forget to monitor them, or give up before the treatment works.

When DIY Isn't Enough: Understanding Kansas Termites

In Kansas, subterranean termites are particularly aggressive due to our soil composition and climate patterns. These termites require contact with soil moisture to survive, which is why they build mud tubes from the ground to wood sources in your home. A mature colony can consume about one pound of wood per day—and your home contains thousands of pounds of wood in floor joists, wall studs, and roof framing.

The structural risk is real. Termites can compromise load-bearing beams before you even notice their presence. By the time most homeowners spot termite swarmers (the winged reproductive termites that emerge in spring), the colony has likely been feeding on the structure for months or years. DIY products might address surface-level problems, but they rarely reach the underground colony or provide the comprehensive barrier protection your home needs.

This is where the cost-benefit calculation shifts. Professional termite treatment in Kansas typically ranges from $1,500 to $3,000 depending on home size and treatment method, and it comes with warranties and guarantees. Homeowners who attempt DIY treatment often spend $300-$600 on products that don't work, then still need to hire professionals—wasting both money and time while termites continue damaging their home. At Shaw's Pest Control, we've treated countless homes where DIY attempts failed, and the additional damage accumulated during those failed attempts increased the overall repair costs significantly.

Termite Control DIY Options in Wichita

If you're a Wichita homeowner dealing with termites, understanding your local risk factors helps you make better decisions. Wichita's combination of clay soils, moderate humidity, and temperature fluctuations creates ideal conditions for Eastern subterranean termites, the dominant species in our area. These termites remain active year-round in Kansas, though swarming season typically peaks from March through May.

Local building practices matter too. Many Wichita homes built before 1990 lack modern termite-resistant construction features like physical barriers, treated lumber, or proper drainage systems. Older homes with crawl spaces, homes with wood-to-ground contact, and properties with drainage issues face the highest termite risk. If your home fits these descriptions, DIY prevention methods like fixing moisture problems, removing wood debris from around your foundation, and ensuring proper drainage can reduce your risk—but they won't eliminate an existing colony.

For Wichita homeowners considering DIY approaches, start with a professional inspection before investing in treatment products. At Shaw's Pest Control, we offer thorough termite inspections that identify the species, locate entry points, and assess damage severity. This information helps you understand whether preventive DIY measures might work or if you're facing an infestation that requires professional intervention. You can reach our team at (316) 251-9461 or through our contact page to schedule an inspection.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you effectively get rid of termites yourself?

You can use DIY methods for termite prevention, but eliminating an active subterranean termite colony yourself is extremely difficult. Borate wood treatments work well for prevention on exposed wood, but they won't eliminate existing colonies. Store-bought barrier treatments rarely achieve the coverage and concentration needed to stop termites completely. Professional treatment remains the most reliable way to eliminate active infestations and protect your home long-term.

What is the most effective DIY termite treatment?

Borate-based wood treatments like Bora-Care or Tim-bor are the most effective DIY termite control option. These products penetrate bare wood and remain effective for years, killing termites that consume treated wood. However, they only work on exposed, untreated wood and don't eliminate existing colonies. For active infestations, professional liquid termiticide treatments or bait systems that target the entire colony are far more effective than any DIY approach.

How much does professional termite treatment cost compared to DIY?

DIY termite control products typically cost $200-$600 for materials, but they rarely eliminate active infestations. Professional treatment in Kansas ranges from $1,500-$3,000 depending on home size, treatment method, and infestation severity. While professional treatment costs more upfront, it includes warranties, guarantees, proper application, and actually eliminates colonies. Most homeowners who try DIY first end up paying for professional treatment anyway, plus additional repair costs from continued termite damage.

Are termite bait stations worth it for DIY use?

Store-bought termite bait stations have limited effectiveness compared to professional systems. While they use similar principles, DIY stations often contain less palatable baits, require perfect placement to intercept termites, and need consistent monitoring for months to work. Most homeowners don't maintain them properly or give them enough time to eliminate colonies. Professional bait systems include superior products, expert placement, regular monitoring, and guaranteed results—making them more cost-effective than DIY alternatives.

When should you call a professional for termite control?

Call a professional immediately if you see termite swarmers (winged termites), find mud tubes on your foundation, discover wood damage with honeycomb patterns, or spot tiny pinholes in drywall. These signs indicate an active infestation that DIY products cannot effectively address. Also call professionals for preventive treatment if you live in a high-risk area, have had termites before, or want comprehensive protection. Early professional intervention costs far less than repairing extensive structural damage from untreated infestations.

What home maintenance helps prevent termites?

Reduce moisture around your foundation by fixing leaky faucets, improving drainage, and keeping gutters clean. Remove wood debris, mulch, and firewood stored against your home's exterior. Eliminate wood-to-ground contact by ensuring siding, deck posts, and stairs don't touch soil. Seal cracks in your foundation and around utility penetrations. These maintenance steps reduce termite attraction but don't eliminate colonies or guarantee protection—they work best combined with professional prevention treatments or borate applications on exposed wood.

Ready to Protect Your Home the Right Way?

DIY termite control has its place—mainly in prevention and protecting exposed wood during construction—but active termite infestations in Kansas require professional expertise. Don't let termites continue damaging your biggest investment while DIY products fail to deliver. Call us at (316) 251-9461 or visit our termite control page to schedule your inspection.
